newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SAfrica budget collection up as personal taxes cut.
newsitem.headline: SAfrica budget collection up as personal taxes cut.

text.p: South African Finance Minister Trevor Manuel on Wednesday announced a 1997/98 revenue target of 161.98 billion rand, including 2.5 billion rand from improved tax collection and net tax relief of 908 million rand.
There are no new taxes and no net tax increases in the 1997/98 budget, which Manuel said would provide tax relief to working people.
The revenue figure is 11.1 percent up on the total for 1996/97 and is equal to 26 percent of gross domestic product.
Manuel said personal tax rates would be restructured at a cost of 2.8 billion rand, mainly to relieve the burden on people earning under 60,000 rand a year.
Manuel said the improved efficiency of the new and autonomous South African Revenue Service would go a long way towards financing the tax breaks.

"Building on the progress made this past year, I am able to include an amount of 2.5 billion rand in the revenue proposals presented today which will arise from improved collections and receipt of arrear taxes," he said.

The changes included an increase in the primary personal rebate to 3,215 rand from 2,660 rand, the elimination of one of the eight existing tax brackets and measures to limit the effect of inflation on lower-income earners.
The Standard Income Tax on Employees (SITE) threshold will increase to 60,000 rand from 50,000 rand, exempting about 470,000 people from the need to complete a detailed tax return.
Manuel said it was too early to estimate the income from a partial tax amnesty which expired at the end of February, but he warned dodgers there would be no further mercy for non-payers.
"We shall actively pursue anyone who breaks the law...we believe that the time has come to stop the rot," he said.
With average wages expected to increase by 11 percent, the government estimated personal tax revenue would increase by 15.7 percent to 66.7 billion rand in fiscal 1997/98.
Gold mine taxes were expected to increase by 32.2 percent to 800 million rand as a result of higher milling and improved profitability on the back of an improved rand gold price.
Taxes on non-mining companies would yield 20.4 billion rand, up 12.7 percent on 1996/97 revenues, Manuel said.
Value added tax (VAT), unchanged at 14 percent, was expected to yield 39.8 billion rand, the major part of 58.1 billion rand expected from domestic taxes on goods and services.
Manuel said VAT on financial services would be abolished from January 1 next year, but would not effect revenues in the current fiscal year.
Manuel announced new restrictions worth over 370 million rand a year on fringe benefits, which he said were being abused at the expense cash-wage earners.
These included an increase from July 1 in the monthly tax on company cars to 1.8 percent of value from 1.2 percent, on a first car and to four percent from two percent on a second car.
The formula used to calculate travel allowances, the taxable value of residential accommodation provided to employees and the provision of holiday accommodation will be tightened.
An adjustment to the application of the 17 percent tax on the interest and rental income of retirement funds will make dividends earned from property investments in mutual funds taxable.
This and a new tax on fees paid by borrowers of financial instruments is expected to yield 200 million rand a year.

The tax on marketable securities and the stamp duty on share transactions will be cut to 0.25 percent from 0.5 percent from April 1 at an estimated cost of around 125 million rand a year. The exemption for foreign residents will be withdrawn.
Ad valorem duties on imported luxury items will be reduced at an estimated cost of 150 million rand with the maximum rate cut to 15 percent from 37.5 percent and most other rates reduced.
"It is anticipated that the lower rates will curb evasion of these duties and that the loss will be partially offset by an increase in declarations," Manuel said.

In the traditional round of increased "sin taxes", Manuel slapped an additional 798 million rand on tobacco and alcohol, including an additional 54 cents on a pack of 20 cigarettes, taking the total tax to 50 percent of the average retail price.
"The news for drinkers is equally sobering," he said, adding that beer would go up by three cents a can, wine by eight cents a bottle and spirits by about 66 cents a bottle.
Four cents per litre of the existing fuel levy to the Equalisation Fund will be applied instead to revenue, yielding 800 million rand to the government without any effect on pump prices.
